title: The Roll of Names (excerpt, Hearthvale)
author: kept at Wardens' Rest; this hand is Pellam Ashcombe's, corrected by Wren Tallow
body:
# The Roll of Names

*Hearthvale. Kept since the Tending. Read aloud on Tollday. Deep lines are read first.*

**Merrowby.** Town. Hearths at last count: 108. Mill, forge, bakery, brewhouse, inn (the Toll's Lip). Seventeen family bells in the lane. *Note in a second hand: sixteen since spring; see Fennick.*

**Tamwick.** Hamlet. Hearths: 19. Orchards, one cider press. *The only apple trees in Wickmere. Do not let the press fail.*

**Wardens' Rest.** Waystation. Hearths: 11, and a cell with a window.

**Larkbourne Ford.** Two cottages and a bridge. Hearths: 2. *The Boys are on this road again. Patrol Tollday and Thornday, not the same hour twice.*

---

## The deep lines

These are read first and read slowly. A Warden reads them. If no Warden is present, whoever is present reads them.

**LARKSTEAD.** Down between the Hound and the scarp. Hearths at last count: 14. Went quiet in the winter of 993. Found empty in the spring; found nothing at all in 997. *A sheep-bell, a boot-scraper and a door were brought back and are in the Roll room. The door is oak and painted green, so: a grower's house.*

**GOSFORD.** Soft ground west of the Larkbourne. Hearths: 9. Stopped sending a cart to market in the eleven days the Toll hummed, in 981. Walked out to by P. Ashcombe, then twenty-two years old, who found a lane, a green, nine houses with the doors on, kettles on hooks and a loom half-finished, and nobody, and no sign of a hurry.

**MULLBOURNE.** Soft ground. Hearths: nine, or eleven; both figures are in this book in the same hand and I will not choose between them. A mill that never worked. A well that tasted of iron. *Line entered 1040. In 1042 the keeper could no longer bring the name to mind at the bell and it has been read from this page since. In 1043 the page was found to be —*

*(Here the page is scraped almost through, not cut. Below, in a newer hand:)*

*I have written it in again from a hearth-tally and an eel-knife. Custom says a found name with nobody living to tend it is written fresh, read aloud once by a Warden, and struck. I have not struck it. Pellam says a struck name is a place that never was. I think Pellam is wrong and I have not been able to hold a pen steadily enough to prove it. — W. Tallow*

**HAREWELL.** Down between Merrowby and Tamwick. Hearths: eleven in 1029, nine in 1030, no figure in 1031 and 'ask Tamwick' written in the margin by a steward who did not, or did and did not write it down. A well with a hare cut on the lip. A woman called Cille who sold hedge-honey on the end stall at Merrowby market.

*Line entered this year. I bought honey from her for six years. I cannot tell you her face and neither can Maud Brambling, who bought from her for twenty. A chalk doorstep was brought back from the down and is in the box. Since it has been in the box the down has not given up the place again.*

*Four lines. I should like it to stay four. — W. Tallow*

title: The First Lecture: On Saying
author: the Sayers' Circle, Tollmere; delivered to Listeners in their first week
body:
# The First Lecture: On Saying

*Read this before you attempt anything. The untrained voice is a hazard to the neighbourhood.*

Saying is speaking the world louder.

It is not command. There are no commands; nothing in Wickmere takes orders. It is not creation. You cannot Say a thing that is not there, and every year a Listener tries, and every year we watch, because watching is cheaper than arguing.

Saying is three motions, and the third is the only hard one.

**Attend.** Look at the thing until you could draw it. Not until you recognise it — until you could draw it. Most failures are here. A Listener who Says *bridge* at a bridge they have glanced at is Saying a word at a word.

**Name.** Say what it is, precisely, in the plainest language you have. Not what it means to you. Not what it resembles. The Circle's records are full of beautiful failures by people who Said *my father's bridge* and got nothing, because the bridge is not that and never was.

**Sustain.** Say it again. And again. Past the point of feeling foolish, which arrives at about the fourth repetition, and past the point of boredom, which arrives at about the fortieth, and into the flat patient place beyond boredom where the work happens. This is why we train at chalk hills and not at objects anyone cares about. The Chalk Hound is very old, very simple, and cannot be offended.

## The three-times rule

A new word is said three times aloud before it is used in a sentence. Students find this comic for a month and then do it for life. The reason is not ceremony. It is that a mouth carrying a word it has not weighed will eventually carry it into a Saying, and a Saying is sustained attention, and sustained attention to a word you do not understand is the definition of the accidents in our records. See: *the bridge at Nauve's Landing, 1011*, and the four pages of consequences.

## What you will not be told for some years

Saying has an inverse and this Circle has used it.

You may attend to a thing and decline to name it, and do so in company, deliberately, sustained, for years. A word withheld by enough mouths for long enough is not silence; it is work, and it is our work, done backwards. The Quiet Hands under the city practise a coarse version and call it Hush and sell it to smugglers.

You will be told that the Circle does not do this. You will be told it by people who believe it.

When you reach the roll of members, and you will, because Listeners always do, you will find a line in the year 941 scraped down to the vellum and written over. Hold it to a lamp. There is a name under it.

It is the Circle's own craft, applied to a colleague, on purpose, because she taught an account we did not want taught in this city. It worked. It is the most successful experiment in our history and it is not written down anywhere, and the woman it was performed on is a ghost under a line of ink.

Attend. Name. Sustain. Begin with the Hound, and understand what you are learning to do.

title: The Vigil Book
author: the Tolling Order, Pilgrim's Ash; read to every new Pilgrim on the first night
body:
# The Vigil Book

*Read on the first night, by whoever is awake. The rule is four lines long. The rest is what we have learned about obeying four lines.*

## The rule

Keep the ring.
Count the bells.
Walk with the ones who are going.
Do not make a fuss.

## On keeping

You will want to do more. Everyone wants to do more, and more than half of those who fail this, fail by doing more. There is nothing out there to be rescued and nothing to be defeated, and a knight who goes hunting in the ash at night is a knight we go out for at dawn.

The ash-wights come up from Greyfold when a bell sounds. They are weak, they are many, they are easily staggered, and **they wave**. Put them down between bells. They were farmers. Say so aloud now and then; it costs nothing and it keeps you the sort of person who can.

## On counting

One bell every few minutes, and nobody rings it. After nineteen years I do not know what rings it, and I have stopped finding that shameful.

So we count. Four hundred and six on the night I write this. If the number changes shape — if there are fewer on a Hushday than a Skerrday, if the gaps lengthen with the season — then someone will have four decades of figures to look at, and that someone will not be me, and that is the correct way round for this work.

The Toll's hum counts as a half. This is disputed. I have argued it with three chapter-masters and won twice.

A counted thing is a kept thing. That is the whole of our theology and we do not have another.

## On walking with them

We do not stop pilgrims. We do not encourage them; the Circle says we do and it is a slander and it is nearly true.

We walk with them to the line so that the last thing they hear is a voice saying something ordinary. Talk about the weather. Talk about the eels. Do not make a speech at the end. If you weep, be kind about it and keep walking.

What they leave at the line, we bring back and hang in the chapter-bell. Once a year, on the night of the Ash Winter, we ring them all at once. It is very loud. It is the only loud thing we do.

## On the founding, which is not what is on the wall

In the Ash Winter, Greyfold's people walked south into the Hush singing. Some walked with them and stopped at the ring and turned back.

A voice in the Seat asked them to. By name. Forty-one names it had never been told, and it asked them to stay and keep count, and eleven stayed, and the rest went on.

That account is in the chapter book in eleven different hands, because nobody could finish writing it at one sitting.

We were founded by the ones who turned back, and we have been ashamed of it for a hundred and seventy-seven years, and we have kept the ring every night of them. Both of those are true. Do not try to resolve it tonight. Count the bells.

— *Cadwen Ash, Toll-Knight*

title: The Rope-Song: the Verse of Kharrow, and the Breath
author: Clan Kharrow; sung, not read. Written at the Sayers' request and under protest.
body:
# The Rope-Song

*Seven verses, one to each clan, sung every morning before food by whoever keeps the memory. Four hundred lines. Here is one verse and the breath that follows it. — D. ko-Kharrow*

## The Verse of Kharrow

Kharrow of the chain and the cut cliff,
who carried a mountain's name up a wall
when the wall had no stair and the name had no keeper.

*The hold:* Kharrow Hold, cut into the gorge face, reached by chain, three hundred years in the cutting and nine in the hanging.

*The dead of note:* Brann ko-Kharrow, who hung the first chain and would not be roped while he did it, and was wrong to refuse, and is sung for anyway. Ushka ko-Kharrow, who kept the memory forty-one years and lost no name. Orrik ko-Kharrow, who went into the Oskeld shaft after his sister and came out, and did not speak again, and is sung for in the same line as those who did not come out, by his own asking.

*The debts unpaid:* to Clan Rudd, for the winter of the long snow, forty head and a hearth; Rudd has been asked three times and has thrice said it is forgiven, and it is not forgiven until we have paid it.

*The debts forgiven:* to Clan Ghast, for blood, in the year of the broken bridge. Forgiven at the Moot. Sung so that it stays forgiven, which is what forgiveness is: a thing you have to keep singing or it comes back.

---

*(Here the singer breathes. This breath is longer than the six others. The scribe has marked its length in the margin: four beats, where the rest are two. — Sayers' note)*

---

## What the breath is

There is no gap in a song. There is only a place where the singer breathes.

Every memory-keeper of Kharrow for a thousand years has taken this breath and none of us has been able to say why, and all of us can say exactly how long. I asked my teacher. She asked hers. It goes back past the asking.

What we hold, which is not sung because it cannot be sung, is this: a clan went down into the Choir when the Choir was new, to sing with the Builders, who were raising a thing to hold the world's note steady. They did not come back. They were breathed in.

What came up the shaft at Oskeld afterwards is their weight without their name. It walks. Half this hold will tell you it is not a person. The other half will not say either way in front of children.

A name is a hand on the rope. Seven clans pull. There should be eight, and the eighth place is kept open by four beats of silence every morning before food, in a hall full of people, none of whom can tell you whose name it is.

We have kept a space open for a thousand years for a name nobody remembers. Your Circle calls that sentiment.

It is the longest-running piece of work in Wickmere, it has been maintained without interruption by people who were never paid for it, and if the name is ever brought up out of that shaft it will go into the song in a single morning and every child in the Hold will have it by winter.

That is what we are for. Write it down if writing helps you.

title: The Round of Sa'oul
author: sung across water at Isseva; taken down by a lantern-maker's daughter
body:
# The Round of Sa'oul

*A round for three voices, sung at the nets and at the burial jetty. The second voice begins when the first reaches the third line. The third voice begins when the second does the same. It does not end; someone stops, and then someone else, and the last voice finishes the line it is on.*

**First voice**

The tide goes out, the tide goes out,
and what it leaves is ours to keep —
the lantern, the eel, the drowned man's boat,
the stone stair going down.

**Second voice**

I will not follow, I will not follow,
I will wait on the boards with my feet in the air,
and mend what came apart in the night,
and mend it again tomorrow.

**Third voice**

Count them, count them, count the small lights,
one for Sa'oul, one for the woman with the nets,
one for the child who went in the reeds —
and one that is nobody's, still burning at dawn.

---

## The lantern-maker's notes

My mother said: do not write this down. I have written it down.

The round is what we sing while working, which is most of the day. It is the reason a reedfolk boat is quiet and a Vale cart is not: we have somewhere to put the noise.

*The apostrophe in Sa'oul* is not decoration. In Sedgish the glottal stop appears only in the names of the drowned. You may hear a stranger say *Saoul* and you will know they have been here less than a season. Nobody corrects them. We simply do not say the name in front of them again.

*The third voice* is the difficult one and children are given it last. It counts the lanterns set out on the water for the dead, and the counting is not for the dead, who are finished; it is done at first light by whoever is eldest, so that somebody knows how many small lights are still going in a direction they cannot see.

*One that is nobody's.* This line is argued about more than anything else on these boards. Some say it is for whoever has died elsewhere unmourned that night. Some say it is for the bell under the peat island that tolls once at midnight and that nobody buried. The eldest of the Council, who is seventy-eight and has put forty-one people into that water, says it is for whoever is listening who has nobody, and that if that is not you tonight, it will be, and the round will still be going.

*On patience.* A Sayer stayed here eleven days once and wrote down that patience was our virtue and fatalism our vice. She was kind and she was half right. The round has no ending because an ending is a thing you plan, and out here you do not plan, you keep the boat mended and the lamp filled and you sing the line you are on.

We taught her the second voice. She had a poor ear and she came back to it every evening for eleven evenings and by the end she could hold it against the first. Then she went home to Tollmere and they scraped her name off a page.

We still sing the second voice the way she sang it, slightly flat, on the fourth line. Nobody in Isseva has ever decided to do that. It is simply how it goes here now.

title: Lantern Row Day-Book: one week of prices
author: Orrin Quill, steward, for the Tallymen of Tollmere
body:
# Lantern Row Day-Book

*Week ending Tollday. Posted on the charter-board at first light each day, as the Charter requires. Marginal notes are the steward's own and are not posted.*

**Kindleday**

- Wharfage, lake barge, chartered: 2 marks. Posted.
- Wharfage, lake barge, unchartered: 11 marks. Posted. *This differential is the Guild's and not mine. See below.*
- Obstruction of the row, barrow left standing, M. Tarrow, carter, of Merrowby: **4 marks**. Paid same day. *Tarrow carries for the Guild's own chandler. Noted because it will be asked.*
- Night watchman, one, hired by the Cooper's hall: 6 marks.

**Tallowday**

- Obstruction of the row, barrow left standing, J. Wick, fisher, of Gullhithe: **40 marks**. Not paid. Distraint on the barrow. *Same street. Same offence. Same week. The reasoning written down is that a fisher's trade is unlicensed and a carter's is chartered. The reasoning is real. It is also a wall built where a wall was wanted.*
- Copying of a deed: 3 marks.
- Fine remitted, affray at the Brass Lamp, two apprentices of the Goldsmiths: 0. *Remitted at the request of the hall. Entered as remitted, which is the Charter's requirement and the Charter's whole virtue; a thing written down as given away is harder to give away twice.*

**Merrowday**

- Licence, itinerant singer, one week: 1 mark. *M. Gosling of Merrowby. Paid in coin and in a verse about the Row which I have declined to have written about me.*
- Toll, Long Stride causeway, cart: 1 mark. Foot: free. *Free since the Charter. The Guild has proposed a foot-toll four times in my service and been refused four times by the Row, which is the best thing about the Row.*
- Search of a warehouse on information: 9 marks, charged to the informant, as the Charter requires. *This is the price of accusing a neighbour and it is the reason we have fewer accusations than Merrowby, which has none, and more grudges than Merrowby, which has all of them.*

**Thornday**

- Watch called to the Undercroft stair: 6 marks, charged to nobody, absorbed. *Nothing found. Nothing is ever found. The door down there has no hinges and does not open for a watchman, which I have written in this book eleven times in nine years.*

**Skerrday**

- Weights inspected, eleven stalls, two condemned: 4 marks each, posted with the names.
- Fine, short measure, third offence, name posted: 30 marks. *Posting the name is worth more than the thirty marks and every stallholder on this row knows it. That is the machine working.*

**Hushday**

- Deed registered, house on Cooper's Lane: 12 marks.
- Fee, reading of the board aloud for those who cannot read, per applicant: **free, and to remain free.** *I have had to defend this line in Guild session twice. If it ever carries a figure, the board is a wall and not a window, and I will say so in session and be heard courteously, and the figure will stand, and I will post it in a large clear hand at first light, because the alternative is not posting it.*

*Totalled and closed. — O. Quill*
